title: Role-based mock interviews
description: Practice clear reasoning with role-specific scenarios and a feedback rubric.
prerequisites: Complete the core lessons in your chosen learning path.
objectives: Structure an answer around assumptions, tradeoffs, and evidence
Practice a role-specific scenario without inventing experience
explanation: A useful technical answer starts by clarifying the task and constraints. State assumptions, propose a simple baseline, explain the design and its tradeoffs, then describe verification and failure handling. Distinguish work you performed from a hypothetical approach you would take.

Match practice to the role. A beginner can explain training versus inference with an everyday example. A developer can design a server-side tool call with validation. An engineer can diagnose retrieval and serving failures. A product manager can define user value, acceptance criteria, and a go/no-go decision.

Use a repeatable mock interview: two minutes to clarify, five to explain, and three for challenges and feedback. Score correctness, structure, evidence, and tradeoff awareness from zero to two each. This rubric is a practice tool, not an employer hiring standard. Repeat the same scenario after reviewing weak areas.

terms.definition: A question that resolves a constraint affecting the proposed solution.
A choice that improves one objective while affecting another.
Specific observations or experience supporting a claim about action or results.

example: For “design a policy assistant,” a developer explains identity, retrieval, citations, and denied access. An engineer adds evaluation and latency budgets. A manager asks who benefits, how review works, and which result would stop the pilot. All roles acknowledge absent evidence.
mistakes: Listing tools without connecting them to requirements.
Claiming hands-on experience with a system you only read about.
Giving precise performance guarantees without measurement.
exercise: Choose a role and record a ten-minute answer to the policy-assistant scenario. Score the four rubric dimensions, identify one missing assumption and one unsupported claim, review the related lessons, and try again.

questions.question: What is a strong first step for an open-ended AI interview scenario?
questions.answer: Clarify the user task, constraints, and success criteria before choosing components.
questions.distractor: Immediately list every framework you know.

questions.question: How should you describe a design you have not implemented?
questions.answer: Label it as a proposed approach and explain how you would validate it.
questions.distractor: Present hypothetical results as measured experience.

questions.question: An interviewer asks whether RAG eliminates hallucinations. What is a sound answer?
questions.answer: No. Retrieval can improve grounding, but evidence selection and unsupported generation still need evaluation.
questions.distractor: Yes, using a vector database guarantees factual answers.

questions.question: What should an engineer discuss when a prototype becomes slow under load?
questions.answer: Queueing, first-token and total latency, concurrency, memory, and measured workload tradeoffs.

questions.question: What should a product manager include in an AI pilot decision?
questions.answer: User outcomes, baseline, review cost, risks, acceptance evidence, and a stop or continue criterion.
questions.distractor: Only whether a popular model was used.
